hello.note: Ẹ is the respectful form for elders and strangers. Casual, to a friend: báwo ni?

goodbye.note: Also common: ó dìgbà (until next time).

please.note: Fuller form: ẹ jọ̀wọ́. To a friend or someone younger: jọ̀ọ́.

thank_you.note: To a friend or someone younger: o ṣé. Also ẹ ṣeun. Thank you very much: ẹ ṣé gan-an.

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'it isn't worth thanks'. Also common: kò sí wàhálà (no trouble).

sorry.note: To a friend: má bínú. Ẹ pẹ̀lẹ́ shows sympathy (someone tripped or is unwell); it is not an apology.

excuse_me.note: Same word as 'please'; the drawn-out o calls attention. Often followed by sà (sir) or mà (ma'am).

good_morning.note: To a friend or someone younger: káàárọ̀. The reply is the same greeting.

how_are_you.note: Casual, to a friend: báwo ni? Also common: ṣé àlàáfíà ni?

im_fine.note: Very common reply: a dúpẹ́ (we give thanks).

whats_your_name.note: In speech often kí lorúkọ yín? To a child or friend: kí ni orúkọ rẹ?

nice_to_meet_you.text: Inú mi dùn láti pàdé yín
nice_to_meet_you.note: To a friend or someone younger: … láti pàdé rẹ.

where_from.note: To a friend or someone younger: ibo lo ti wá?

im_from.note: Also natural, stressing the place: … ni mo ti wá.

speak_english.note: Also common: ṣé ẹ gbọ́ Gẹ̀ẹ́sì? (do you understand English?)

speak_slowly.note: Please say it again: ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ tún un sọ.

where.note: Also ibo? Where is …?: ibo ni … wà?

what.note: Pardon, what did you say?: kí lẹ sọ?

why.note: Also means 'what's wrong?'. More formal: nítorí kí ni?

how_much.note: In quick market speech: èló lèyí? Bargaining is normal.

where_bathroom.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ibo ni ilé ìgbọ̀nsẹ̀ wà?
where_bathroom.note: Many people simply use the English word toilet. Balùwẹ̀ is a room for bathing.

can_you_help.text: Ṣé ẹ lè ràn mí lọ́wọ́?

what_time.note: Answer, e.g.: aago mẹ́ta ló lù (it's three o'clock).

one.note: After a noun: kan (ìwé kan, one book).

two.note: After a noun: méjì (ìwé méjì, two books).

three.note: After a noun: mẹ́ta (ìwé mẹ́ta, three books).

four.note: After a noun: mẹ́rin (ìwé mẹ́rin, four books).

five.note: After a noun: márùn-ún (ìwé márùn-ún, five books).

six.note: After a noun: mẹ́fà (ìwé mẹ́fà, six books).

seven.note: After a noun: méje (ìwé méje, seven books).

eight.note: After a noun: mẹ́jọ (ìwé mẹ́jọ, eight books).

nine.note: After a noun: mẹ́sàn-án (ìwé mẹ́sàn-án, nine books).

ten.note: After a noun: mẹ́wàá (ìwé mẹ́wàá, ten books).

tea.note: In Nigeria tíì can mean any hot drink, including cocoa drinks.

im_hungry.note: Literally 'hunger is killing me'. I'm thirsty: òùngbẹ ń gbẹ mí.

menu_please.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ fún mi ní mẹ́nù
menu_please.note: A local bùkà rarely has a menu; ask kí lẹ ní? (what do you have?)

bill_please.text: Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, èló ni gbogbo rẹ̀?
bill_please.note: Literally 'how much is it all?', the usual way to ask for the bill.

delicious.note: Very tasty: ó dùn gan-an! Dùn also means sweet or pleasant.

no_meat.note: Fish (ẹja) is often not counted as meat; add mi kì í jẹ ẹja if needed.

enjoy_meal.note: To a friend: gbádùn oúnjẹ rẹ! People eating often invite you: ẹ wá jẹun (come and eat).

left.note: Turn left: ẹ yà sí òsì.

right.note: Turn right: ẹ yà sí ọ̀tún.

straight_ahead.note: Go straight on: ẹ máa lọ tààrà.

airport.note: In everyday speech the English word airport is also common.

train_station.note: The train itself: ọkọ̀ ojú irin.

want_to_go.note: Sí merges with a following vowel: lọ sí ilé → lọ sílé (go home).

is_it_far.note: Replies: ó jìnnà (it's far), kò jìnnà (it's not far).

too_expensive.note: Bargaining is expected: ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ dín in kù (please bring the price down).

cheaper.text: Ṣé ẹ ní èyí tí kò wọ́n tó báyìí?

id_like_this.note: Also natural: èyí ni mo fẹ́ (this is the one I want).

pay_card.text: Ṣé mo lè fi káàdì sanwó?
pay_card.note: In Nigeria people often ask: ṣé ẹ ní POS? (do you have a card machine?)

cash.note: Many people simply say the English word cash. Bank transfers are also very common.

open.note: Shop signs in Nigeria are nearly always in English.

closed.note: We've closed for the day: a ti tì. Shop signs are nearly always in English.

big.note: After a noun: ilé ńlá (a big house). It's big: ó tóbi.

small.note: After a noun: ilé kékeré (a small house). It's small: ó kéré.

today.note: Inside a sentence: lónìí, e.g. mo máa lọ lónìí (I'll go today).

later.note: Often shortened to tó bá yá.

good_evening.note: To a friend: káalẹ́. In the afternoon: ẹ káàsán.

good_night.note: Also: ẹ sùn re o (sleep well).

wait_moment.note: Dúró means wait, stop and stand.

need_doctor.note: Also common: mo fẹ́ rí dókítà (I want to see a doctor).

im_lost.note: Also: ọ̀nà ti dà mí rú (I've got mixed up about the way).

dont_feel_well.note: Careful form: ara mi kò yá.

pharmacy.note: In everyday speech most people say chemist, borrowed from English.

lost_phone.text: Mo ti sọ fóònù mi nù
lost_phone.note: If it was stolen: wọ́n ti jí fóònù mi.

allergic.note: People also use the English word allergy.

i_like_it.note: Of something you see and fancy: ó wù mí.

dont_like_it.note: Of something you see: kò wù mí.

welcome.note: To a friend or someone younger: káàbọ̀.
